title: The colour wheel: primary, secondary and tertiary colours
examples: How does a colour wheel work?

stages.label: Red
stages.note: Primary: you cannot mix it from others

explain.say: Imagine taking a rainbow and bending it round into a circle, so red meets violet. That is a colour wheel, a map that shows how colours are related. Look at the board: six colours, each sitting next to its neighbours.

draw.text: The colour wheel: primary, secondary and tertiary colours

stages.label: Red
stages.note: Primary: you cannot mix it from others

explain.say: Look at red. Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours for paint. Primary means first: you cannot mix them from other paints, but you can mix almost everything else from them. Can you spot the other two primaries on the wheel?

stages.label: Red
stages.note: Primary: you cannot mix it from others

explain.say: Now look at orange, between red and yellow. Mix two primaries and you get a secondary colour: red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, blue and red make violet. Mix a primary with its secondary neighbour, like yellow and green, and you get a tertiary colour, yellow-green. What is between blue and violet?

stages.label: Red
stages.note: Primary: you cannot mix it from others

explain.say: Look at blue, then look straight across the circle: orange! Colours opposite each other are called complementary colours. Side by side they make each other look brighter, which is why sports kits and posters love them. What is opposite red?

stages.label: Red
stages.note: Primary: you cannot mix it from others

explain.say: Yes, green! Brilliant work. Wow fact: Isaac Newton drew one of the first colour wheels in 1704, after splitting sunlight into a rainbow with a glass prism. Challenge: find two complementary colours on a flag, a shop sign or a book cover today.

stages.label: Red
stages.note: Primary: you cannot mix it from others

faq.a: In paint, the traditional primary colours are red, yellow and blue. They cannot be mixed from other paints, and they mix to make many other colours.
asks: Why are red yellow and blue primary?

faq.a: Secondary colours are made by mixing two primary colours: red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, and blue and red make violet, or purple.
asks: How do you make secondary colours?

faq.a: Tertiary colours are made by mixing a primary colour with the secondary colour next to it, such as red-orange, yellow-green or blue-violet. The wheel then has 12 colours.
asks: How many colours on a 12-part colour wheel?

faq.a: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the colour wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet. Next to each other they look extra bright and bold.
asks: Why do opposite colours stand out?

faq.q: Who made the first colour wheel?
faq.a: Isaac Newton published one of the first colour circles in his book Opticks in 1704, bending the colours of the rainbow into a circle.
asks: When was the colour wheel invented?
Did Newton invent the colour wheel?

facts: Isaac Newton arranged the colours of the spectrum in a circle in his book Opticks, published in 1704.
On the traditional painter's colour wheel, complementary pairs are red and green, blue and orange, and yellow and violet.

quiz.say: Which two primary colours mix to make green?
quiz.why: Green sits between yellow and blue on the wheel, and those two mix to make it.

wrong.2: Red and blue make violet, or purple.

quiz.say: Which colour is the complement of orange, opposite it on the wheel?
quiz.why: Blue sits straight across the colour wheel from orange.

wrong.1: Red is next to orange, not opposite it.
wrong.2: Yellow is next to orange; its opposite is violet.
